one_liner: Header-only AVX-512 quicksort with bitonic small-sort for int, double and int key/value arrays; paper claims 4x over GNU std::sort.
what_it_does: Sorts contiguous arrays of int or double (sort512.hpp) and int keys with a parallel int values array (sort512kv.hpp) in ascending order, in place, on CPUs with AVX-512F. The API is free functions over a raw pointer and a count, Sort512::Sort<T, IndexType>(array, size) and Sort512kv::Sort(keys, values, size), plus building blocks (Partition512, SmallSort16V) and OpenMP variants (SortOmpPartition, SortOmpMerge, SortOmpMergeDeps, SortOmpParMerge). It is not a drop-in for std::sort: no iterators, no comparator, no other key types.
how_it_is_fast: Quicksort whose partition step loads 512-bit vectors from both ends, compares them against a broadcast pivot into a mask, and writes the low and high lanes with masked compress-stores (_mm512_mask_compressstoreu), so partitioning is branch-free except for choosing which end to read next. Subarrays under 16 vectors (256 ints or 128 doubles) go to fully unrolled bitonic sorting networks built from permutexvar plus min/max, with the last partial vector padded with INT_MAX or DBL_MAX. The pivot is a scalar median of three; master's Sort corresponds to the paper branch's NewQuickSort512V5.
when_to_use: Single-threaded sorting of large arrays of 32-bit int or double keys that are close to distinct (random data, IDs, measurements) on Intel AVX-512 hardware (Skylake-SP/X and later, or Knights Landing).
Sorting int keys with an int payload stored in a separate array (struct-of-arrays layout) without packing pairs.
As a small, MIT-licensed, readable reference for the AVX-512 compress-store partition plus bitonic-network design that later libraries (numpy/x86-simd-sort cites it) refined.
Sorting many short arrays (up to 256 ints or 128 doubles) with SmallSort16V's branch-free networks.
when_not_to_use: Inputs with many duplicate keys: the <= pivot partition sends every element equal to the pivot left, so an all-equal run shrinks by one element per level and the sort becomes O(n^2) (issue #1, closed 2022-03-27 without a code change; the author suggests an is_sorted pre-check, which does not help low-cardinality data that is not all equal).

Doubles that may contain +infinity or NaN: the padding value DBL_MAX sorts below +inf, so +inf values in a leaf block whose length is not a multiple of 8 are overwritten with DBL_MAX, and NaN ordering is undefined (min/max and _CMP_LE_OQ semantics).
Machines without AVX-512F (any AVX2-only x86, Arm): there is no fallback; the Arm SVE variant lives in a separate gitlab.inria.fr repository.
Code that needs a comparator, iterators, 64-bit integer keys, stability or adversarial-input guarantees (no introsort fallback, median-of-three pivot only).
New projects that want maintenance: numpy/x86-simd-sort and Highway vqsort are maintained successors covering more types and duplicate-heavy inputs.

integration.dependencies: none for the sequential sort (immintrin.h); OpenMP and the bundled parallelInplace.hpp for the parallel variants
integration.min_toolchain: C++11 (build lines use -std=c++11); GCC with -mavx512f -mavx512cd (plus -mavx512vl -mavx512bw -mavx512dq for Skylake) or icpc -xCORE-AVX512; CI used GCC 6
integration.platforms: x86-64 with AVX-512F (Intel Knights Landing and Skylake were the targets); no non-AVX-512 path
integration.thread_safety: not documented; the sequential functions keep no shared state, so concurrent calls on different arrays are independent by construction
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: replaces std::sort(p, p + n) for plain int or double arrays in ascending order only, with a different call (Sort512::Sort(p, n)) and without comparator, iterator, duplicate-heavy or special-float safety

gotchas: Sort512::Sort with IndexType size_t and size 0 computes right = size - 1 = SIZE_MAX, skips the small-sort branch and reads array[SIZE_MAX/2] while choosing the pivot (out-of-bounds read); the unit tests start at size 1. Guard empty inputs yourself.

Duplicate-key and special-value pathologies above are not caught by the tests: sort512test.cpp only sorts power-of-two sizes up to 1024 filled with drand48()*size values, and the benchmark (paper-branch timeAll, master sort512perf.cpp) uses the same near-distinct uniform random input, so the published speedups never exercise the O(n^2) duplicate case.

SortOmpMerge and SortOmpParMerge need a power-of-two thread count, but the assert sits outside the parallel region where omp_get_num_threads() is 1 (and -DNDEBUG removes it); with 6 threads, thread 4 spins forever on done[1][3], a flag only a nonexistent thread 6 would set. Use SortOmpPartition or set OMP_NUM_THREADS to a power of two (at most 128).

The README and header still name Sort512::SortOmp(), which no longer exists after the July 2020 strategy split; the master commit of 2022-06-20 changed signed-zero handling in the min/max networks after the paper's measurements.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over WojciechMula/simd-sort when you need doubles or int key/value pairs as well as int32 keys from one header, and over jonicho/simd-radix-sort when you want a comparison-based in-place quicksort rather than an MSB radix sort; for anything new, numpy/x86-simd-sort (wave 1) is the maintained successor of this design.
verified_claims_summary: The IJACSA 2017 paper (arXiv 1704.08579, abstract seen in search snippets only) reports about 4x over GNU std::sort with a lambda less-than and about 1.4x over Intel IPP ippsSortRadixAscend on a Skylake Xeon whose model, like the compiler version, is not confirmed; the paper-branch harness behind it times single-threaded sorts of drand48()*n int and double arrays from 64 to 2^30 elements in x8 steps, regenerating identical input for each algorithm and averaging 5 runs.
status_note: Abandoned since the 2022-06-20 signed-zero fix (29 stars, MIT, header-only and easy to vendor), but its duplicate-key quadratic case and +inf padding bug make it safe only for near-distinct finite keys.
